books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: John L. O’Sullivan, “Annexation,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review (1845)

stimulus.source_note: John L. O’Sullivan, “Annexation,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, 1845; public domain.
stimulus.text:
“. . . other nations have undertaken to intrude themselves . . . in a spirit of hostile interference against us, for the avowed object of thwarting our policy and hampering our power, limiting our greatness and checking the fulfillment of our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions.”
— John L. O’Sullivan, “Annexation,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, 1845

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from John L. O’Sullivan, “Annexation” (1845), public domain
stem: A historian writing about why the United States went to war with itself in 1861 would most likely use this passage as evidence that

options.text: most Northerners in 1845 were committed abolitionists who wanted slavery ended at once, everywhere in the Union, by law and without compensation.
options.misconception: The books note abolitionism was a minority position in the North in 1850; the passage says nothing about abolition.

options.text: ideas about a God-given mission to expand drove the taking of new land, which forced the nation to decide whether slavery would spread.
the annexation of Texas was opposed by every American political party and every newspaper in 1845, without a single voice in favor.
options.misconception: The passage itself argues for annexation, and Polk won the 1844 election promising it.

options.text: the United States planned to conquer Canada as well as Mexico in the 1840s, and then to take Cuba too, by force.
options.misconception: O’Sullivan writes about Texas and the continent’s westward spread, not about conquering Canada.

rationales.A: O’Sullivan writes about expansion, not abolition, and abolitionists were a minority in the North.
rationales.B: O’Sullivan gives expansion a holy purpose, and the land his idea helped win raised the question the passage never answers: would slavery go into it? Background from the books: the acquisition of new territories opened the question politicians had tried to avoid, and by the end of the 1850s positions on it had hardened on both sides.
rationales.C: The Democrats under Polk backed annexation, so it was not opposed by every party.
rationales.D: Canada is never named in the passage; the land in question is Texas and the West.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the idea. O’Sullivan says God gave the continent to Americans for their “free development.”
2. Ask what the idea justified. It justified taking Texas, then fighting Mexico for the Southwest.
3. Ask what the new land forced. Every acre raised the question of whether slavery would go into it, and the books say that question split national politics.
4. Reach the war. By the end of the 1850s, positions had hardened until the nation broke apart.
Remember: an idea that wins land can also raise a question that breaks a country.
